section.title: I Know That My Redeemer Lives
section.sectionRationale: This chapter holds the highest peak of hope in the entire book. Job describes feeling utterly abandoned, by God, by his family, by his friends, and then, without warning, breaks into the boldest declaration of faith in all his speeches: he knows his Redeemer lives, and will one day stand on the earth, and that Job himself will see God with his own eyes. It is a hope reached for in the dark, not after the dark has lifted.
section.thesis: Job's isolation is now total, mocked by strangers and abandoned by his own family, yet in the depth of that isolation he reaches his highest confession of hope: a living Redeemer who will one day stand on the earth and before whom Job himself will stand, vindicated, in his own flesh.
section.frameNote: Six movements: Job's renewed rebuke of his friends for tormenting him without cause; his complaint that God has besieged him like an enemy in war; his lament that even his family and closest friends now treat him as a stranger; his raw plea for their pity, since the hand of God has struck him; his climactic declaration, I know that my Redeemer lives, and I will see God in my flesh; and his closing warning that his accusers should themselves fear judgment.

units.label: How long will you torment me?

verses.text: Then Job answered:
"How long will you torment me and crush me with your words?
Ten times now you have reproached me; you shamelessly mistreat me.
Even if I have truly gone astray, my error concerns me alone.
If indeed you would exalt yourselves above me and use my disgrace against me,
then understand that it is God who has wronged me and drawn His net around me.

units.label: God has wronged me
units.note: He has veiled my paths with darkness

verses.text: "Though I cry out, 'Violence!' I get no response; though I call for help, there is no justice.
He has blocked my way so I cannot pass; He has veiled my paths with darkness.
He has stripped me of my honor and removed the crown from my head.
He tears me down on every side until I am gone; He uproots my hope like a tree.
His anger burns against me, and He counts me among His enemies.

His troops advance together; they construct a ramp against me 
and encamp around my tent.

units.label: My own family has turned against me
units.note: I am loathsome to my own family

verses.text: "He has removed my brothers from me; my acquaintances have abandoned me.
My kinsmen have failed me, and my friends have forgotten me.
My guests and maidservants count me as a stranger; I am a foreigner in their sight.
I call for my servant, but he does not answer, though I implore him with my own mouth.
My breath is repulsive to my wife, and I am loathsome to my own family.
Even little boys scorn me; when I appear, they deride me.
All my best friends despise me, and those I love have turned against me.
My skin and flesh cling to my bones; I have escaped by the skin of my teeth.

units.label: Have pity on me, my friends
units.note: the hand of God has struck me

verses.text: "Have pity on me, my friends, have pity, for the hand of God has struck me.
Why do you persecute me as God does? Will you never get enough of my flesh?

units.label: I know that my Redeemer lives
units.note: in my flesh I will see God

verses.text: "I wish that my words were recorded and inscribed in a book,
by an iron stylus on lead, or {{chaqaq|chiseled}} in stone forever.
But I know that my {{goel|Redeemer}} lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth.
Even after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my {{basar|flesh}} I will see God.

I will see Him for myself; my eyes will behold Him, and not as a stranger. 
How my heart {{kalah|yearns}} within me!

units.label: You should fear the sword yourselves

verses.text: "If you say, 'Let us persecute him, since the root of the matter lies with him,'

then you should fear the sword yourselves, because wrath brings punishment by the sword, 
so that you may know there is a judgment."

chaqaq.gloss: To engrave, inscribe, cut permanently into stone or metal. Job wishes his words could be preserved this way forever, a longing that, remarkably, has been fulfilled: this very speech has in fact been engraved in Scripture and read for millennia, outliving every one of the friends who mocked him.

goel.gloss: Redeemer, kinsman-redeemer, one with the right and duty to rescue, avenge, or buy back a relative in distress, as in the book of Ruth. Job's declaration that his go'el lives and will stand on the earth is one of the boldest hopes in the Old Testament, reaching for a living vindicator even while surrounded by loss and isolation.

basar.gloss: Flesh, body, the physical substance of a living person. Job insists that even after his skin, his basar, is destroyed, he will still see God in his flesh, a hope that reaches toward bodily vindication rather than a merely spiritual or disembodied comfort.

kalah.gloss: To be consumed, to yearn, to long intensely to the point of exhaustion. Job's closing exclamation, how my heart yearns within me, captures the overwhelming emotional weight of his hope, longing so deeply for that promised sight of God that his whole being is consumed by it.

basic.context: Job's isolation has become total. Not only do his friends torment him, but his own family, servants, and closest companions now treat him as a stranger; even children mock him. He begs his friends simply to have pity, since God's own hand has struck him. Then, without any narrative preparation, Job reaches the highest point of hope in the entire book: I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth, and even after my body is destroyed, I will see God in my own flesh. He closes by warning his accusers that they, not he, should fear coming judgment.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter should not be flattened into a simple prediction of Jesus that Job fully understood; Job himself does not have New Testament clarity about the resurrection or the incarnation. What he does have is a genuine, Spirit-given hope in a living, vindicating kinsman-redeemer who will one day stand on the earth on his behalf, and a hope that this vindication will include his own body, not merely his soul. The New Testament reveals with full clarity what Job here reaches for by faith in the dark.
basic.originalLanguages: Job's go'el, kinsman-redeemer, is the same office described in Ruth, one with family right and duty to rescue a relative in distress; Job applies this legal and family category to God Himself. He insists this vindication will happen in his basar, flesh, not apart from his body, and his closing cry uses kalah, to be consumed with yearning, showing the sheer emotional weight this hope carries for him.
basic.typology: Job's living Redeemer who will one day stand upon the earth anticipates Christ, who is both kinsman, taking on human flesh, and Redeemer, purchasing His people at the cost of His own blood. Job's hope of seeing God in his own flesh, even after his body is destroyed, anticipates the doctrine of bodily resurrection that the New Testament will reveal in full light.
basic.christ: Job's cry, I know that my Redeemer lives, names by faith what the gospel names by sight: Jesus Christ, our kinsman by His incarnation and our Redeemer by His death and resurrection, who has indeed stood, and will stand again, upon the earth. Job hoped to see God in his own flesh after his body was destroyed; the resurrection of Christ, the firstfruits of all who sleep, guarantees exactly this hope for every believer, not as a vague spiritual comfort but as bodily, physical vindication.
basic.god: God is both the one Job accuses of wronging him, drawing a net around him, and the one whose living presence Job trusts will ultimately vindicate him. This is the same tension seen throughout the dialogue, held together without resolution: a God experienced as adversary in present suffering and trusted as Redeemer in ultimate outcome.
basic.crossReferences: Ruth 4:1-10 shows the kinsman-redeemer, go'el, rescuing a family in distress, the legal background behind Job's hope; 1 Corinthians 15:20 names Christ the firstfruits of the resurrection of the dead; Revelation 1:17-18 shows the risen Christ standing, alive forevermore, holding the keys of death and Hades.
basic.oneStory: In the depth of total isolation, Job reaches the book's highest peak of hope: a living Redeemer who will stand upon the earth and before whom Job will stand vindicated, in his own flesh. This hope, reached for in darkness rather than after it lifted, finds its full and certain answer in Jesus Christ, our kinsman-Redeemer, risen bodily and coming again to stand upon the earth.

context.literary:
Job 19 is the centre of the second round of debate, and it is built like a set of concentric circles closing in on a single point of light. Verses 2 to 6 are an outburst at the friends. Verses 7 to 12 turn to God, the enemy who besieges Job. Verses 13 to 20 turn to the human world, and here the poem moves in a careful pattern: brothers and acquaintances, kinsmen and friends, guests and maidservants, then the servant in his own house, then his wife and family, then children, then his closest friends. It starts at the edge of his circle and moves inward, until even the household turns away. Verses 21 to 22 are a plea, and the shortest in the chapter. Then in 23 to 27 the poem opens into hope, and it closes in 28 to 29 with a warning back to the friends.

The hope in verses 23 to 27 has its own careful structure. It begins with two wishes, "Oh that my words were written" and "Oh that they were engraved", and these follow the formula of longing that Job has used for a mediator and for a hiding place in Sheol. Then the grammar changes: "But I know". A wish gives way to a claim. The three uses of "see" in verses 26 and 27 press the point: I will see God, I will see him for myself, my eyes will behold him.

The chapter also answers the previous speech line by line. Bildad had spoken of nets and traps, and Job says it is God who has drawn His net around him, verse 6. Bildad had begun with "How long", 18:2, and Job opens with it too. Bildad had said the wicked man is forgotten and has no name, and Job asks that his own words be carved in stone so that they will be remembered.

The last two verses turn the sword back on the accusers. What began as a plea for pity ends as a warning, and the reader is left to weigh a hope so high beside a threat so plain.
context.historical:
The go'el at the heart of this chapter belongs to the family law of Israel. When a man fell into poverty, the nearest of kin might redeem the land he had sold, Leviticus 25:25, and if he sold himself into slavery, a brother, uncle or cousin could buy him back, Leviticus 25:47 to 49. When a man was murdered, the avenger of blood stood ready to pursue the killer, Numbers 35:19. In Ruth the go'el takes on a widow's cause, and the women praise the LORD who has not left Naomi without a kinsman-redeemer, Ruth 4:14. In each case the redeemer is the person who steps in when the family is helpless.

The setting of the book is patriarchal, with Job as the head of a large household who offers sacrifices for his own children. To such a man, the losses in verses 13 to 19 are the collapse of his whole social order: brothers, dependants, servants, guests and the wife who had once been at his side. Skin disease also brought exclusion. Leviticus 13:45 to 46 tells the diseased to live outside the camp, and Job's complaint that even his breath is repulsive to his wife fits a sufferer whom others avoid.

The wish to write his words down draws on ancient practice. Kings and lawgivers fixed their records by cutting into stone with iron tools, and lead was used for inscriptions too, so the image of an iron stylus on lead, or chiseled in stone, speaks of the most lasting record then possible. Job wants his claim on the record beyond his own lifetime, for a witness who has not yet been born.

Siege language in verse 12, with a ramp built against the tent, comes from the warfare of walled cities. The same device is named in 2 Kings 19:32, where the LORD promises that the king of Assyria will not build a siege ramp against Jerusalem. Job pictures God as an army encamped around a single tent.
context.canonical:
Job 19:25 to 27 stands at the head of a long line of hope in the Old Testament that the grave is not the end. Job has already asked in 14:14 whether a man who dies will live again, and in 14:13 to 15 he has pictured being hidden in Sheol until God remembers him and calls. Here that question becomes a confession. Psalm 49:15 declares that God will redeem the psalmist's life from Sheol, and Psalm 73:24 says God will later receive him in glory. Isaiah 26:19 promises that the dead will live and their bodies rise, and Daniel 12:2 says that many who sleep in the dust will awake.

The New Testament takes up the hope and names its ground. Christ is 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep', 1 Corinthians 15:20, and the perishable will be clothed with the imperishable, 1 Corinthians 15:53. Paul says that the Lord Jesus Christ will 'transform our lowly bodies' to be like His glorious body, Philippians 3:21. Jesus says the hour is coming when all in their graves will hear His voice and come out, John 5:28 to 29, and after His resurrection He shows His disciples His hands and feet and says a spirit does not have flesh and bones, Luke 24:39.

The hope of seeing God is also a major biblical theme. 'Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God', Matthew 5:8. 'We will see Him as He is', 1 John 3:2. 'They will see His face', Revelation 22:4. The book of Job ends with a first fulfilment, when Job says, 'now my eyes have seen You', Job 42:5.

The word redeemer, go'el, also reaches beyond the family. God is called Redeemer of Israel in Isaiah 41:14 and 54:5, and His redeeming work at the exodus is described with the same verb, Exodus 6:6. The New Testament says Christ redeemed us, Titus 2:14, and did so with 'the precious blood of Christ', 1 Peter 1:18 to 19. Christians have long read Job 19:25 to 27 at funerals and in the church's music as a confession of that hope.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer places this confession where it is least expected. Job is at the lowest point of his social fall, cut off by every circle of relationship, and it is there that he speaks with the most certainty. The order matters. The book does not first solve the problem and then let Job rejoice. The confidence comes while the wound is open.

The writer means the hearer to see what Job's hope is fixed on. It is not on the return of health or of children, and it is not on winning the argument with the friends. It is on a person who lives, who will stand up, and whom Job will see for himself. Job's trust has become personal. He does not say that justice will prevail; he says his Redeemer lives.

The speech is also a rebuke to the friends. They had offered a doctrine that ends in the grave. Job replies with a hope that reaches beyond it. Their warning about the wicked man's memory perishing is answered by a request to be remembered, and their cold certainty by a warm one. The last verses turn the accusation around: those who persecute the innocent should fear a judgment of their own.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records a confession, not a command, and it records it as Job's own. He does not tell his friends that they must believe it, and the book never turns it into a rule for how sufferers should feel. What it describes is what faith can do when it has nothing left but God.

It should not be treated as a formula for cheerful endings. Job says he knows his Redeemer lives, but the book does not say his pain stopped there. The next speech, chapter 20, is Zophar's, and Job's darkest words are still to come. Believers who read the passage should expect that hope may arrive in the middle of unresolved distress and stay next to it.

The passage also does not prescribe how much Job understood. It is fair to say the words point toward the bodily hope of the New Testament, but a reader should not put the whole doctrine of resurrection into Job's mouth. What the text prescribes for us is more modest and more practical: keep hold of the living God, ask for a witness, and refuse to let the accusations of others have the last word.

debates.question: When and how will Job see God, in 19:26?

views.label: In the resurrection, in his own flesh
views.case: The BSB reads 'yet in my flesh I will see God', and the emphasis on 'for myself' and 'my eyes' in verse 27 suggests a bodily seeing after the skin has been destroyed. This is the reading of the Latin Vulgate, of many church fathers and of most Christian tradition, and it fits the hope of Job 14:14.

views.label: After death, apart from his flesh
views.case: The Hebrew preposition can mean 'from' as well as 'in', and the BSB footnote notes the alternative 'without my flesh'. On this reading Job expects to see God after death, as a disembodied person, but not in a risen body. It fits Psalm 73:24.

views.label: In this life, in vindication
views.case: Some take the words as the hope that God will appear before Job dies and clear his name. Job 42:5, 'now my eyes have seen You', is offered as a fulfilment. The phrase 'after my skin has been destroyed' is then read as a figure for his ruined body.

debates.bearing: The first reading has the most support in the grammar of the verses and in later Christian use, but the text is hard, and a careful reader will hold that reading with some humility. All three views agree on what matters: Job expects to meet God as a friend and not as a stranger, and to be vindicated in that meeting.

debates.question: Who is the Redeemer, and what does it mean that He will 'stand upon the earth'?

views.label: God Himself
views.case: The office of go'el is applied to the LORD elsewhere, Isaiah 41:14, and verse 26 goes straight on to say that Job will see God. In 16:19 the witness is in heaven, and here the Redeemer lives. Many take the two as the same figure, God appealed to against God.

views.label: A distinct heavenly figure
views.case: Since Job also longs for a mediator who is not the accused, 9:33, some see a separate advocate. The Redeemer would then be a heavenly ally, and God the one Job finally sees. This keeps the courtroom picture consistent.

views.label: Christ, seen through the whole canon
views.case: Christian readers hear in the Redeemer the person who was born of a woman to redeem, Galatians 4:4 to 5, and who rose in the flesh. This does not deny the first views but reads them in the light of the fulfilment.

debates.bearing: The Hebrew says he will 'stand', a word used for a witness who rises to speak in court, and the place is 'upon the dust', which is where Job lies. The Redeemer comes down to the place of the dead. That picture fits the gospel more than any other, even if Job could not have named it.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb behind "wronged" in verse 6 is the word for twisting or perverting. It is the same verb Bildad used in 8:3 when he asked, "Does God pervert justice?" Bildad expected the answer no. Job now gives the opposite answer. Whatever we make of Job's verdict, the repetition shows that this chapter is the direct reply to a question the friends thought closed.

In verse 7 Job cries, "Violence!", using the Hebrew chamas. It is the word he used in 16:17 when he said his hands were free of violence, and it is the cry of Habakkuk 1:2, 'Violence!' but You do not save. Job cries for help against a wrong and hears no answer. The word ties the chapters together: in 16 he denied doing it, in 19 he cries out against having it done to him.

The verb for "uproots" in verse 10 is applied to his hope, and the noun for hope is the one Job used in 14:7 when he said, "there is hope for a tree." A tree that is cut down may sprout again, Job said. Now he says God has torn up his hope like a tree. The image is the same, the conclusion reversed. It also sets up the surprise of verse 25: the tree has no hope, but the man does, because his hope is not in the tree.

A quiet thread of "strangeness" runs through the family scene and into the climax. In verse 15 the maidservants count him a stranger and a foreigner. In verse 17 his breath is "strange" to his wife. The word in these verses shares a root with the word Job uses in verse 27 when he says he will see God "and not as a stranger". The last phrase can be read two ways, that God will not be a stranger to him, or that he will not be treated as a stranger by God. Either way, the estrangement of the chapter is answered by its reverse.

In verse 25 the phrase "in the end" translates a word that means last, the same word as in Isaiah 44:6, where the LORD says, "I am the first and I am the last." Some readers take Job's line as a title, so that his Redeemer is the Last One, though the natural sense is simply that He will have the last word. The verb "stand" is the word for rising up, and it is used of a witness who takes the stand against someone, Deuteronomy 19:16.

The place is "upon the earth", which can also be "upon the dust". Job used the word in 17:16, asking whether he and his hope will go down together to the dust. The BSB footnote adds "or on my grave". The Redeemer takes his stand precisely on the ground where Job lies buried.

Finally, the BSB footnote to verse 27 records that the Hebrew reads "my kidneys yearn". In 16:13 God "pierces my kidneys", and here the same inner organ is the seat of longing. The part of Job that God's arrows struck is the part that now aches for God.

typology.fulfillment: Boaz stepped into a family's helplessness, bought the land and took the widow, Ruth 4:9 to 10. Job's Redeemer is a living figure who will act for him. The pattern is fulfilled in Christ, who shared our flesh and blood, Hebrews 2:14, was 'born of a woman' to redeem, Galatians 4:4 to 5, and paid with His own blood, 1 Peter 1:18 to 19. The escalation is from redeeming land or a name to redeeming a life from death. The type falls short in that Boaz redeemed at a price he could afford. Christ paid a price no one else could, and for people who were not His kin by nature.

Job is a stranger to his brothers, and even those he loves have turned on him. Psalm 69:8 says, 'I have become a stranger to my brothers and a foreigner to my mother's sons', and John notes that not even Jesus' own brothers believed in Him, John 7:5. At Gethsemane 'everyone deserted Him and fled', Mark 14:50. The pattern is of the righteous one abandoned by those closest to him. It escalates because Jesus was abandoned in bearing the sin of the many, Isaiah 53:12. The type falls short, since Job's isolation carried no atoning purpose.

typology.type: Seeing God in the flesh, 19:26 to 27
typology.fulfillment: Job hopes to see God with his own eyes and in his own flesh. The risen Christ shows His disciples His hands and feet and says a spirit does not have flesh and bones, Luke 24:39, and He is 'the firstfruits', 1 Corinthians 15:20. Believers will be changed to be like Him, and 'we will see Him as He is', 1 John 3:2. The escalation is that the God Job hoped to see has taken flesh, John 1:14, and a body has already been raised. The type falls short only in that Job's hope was for one man, while Christ's resurrection guarantees a harvest.

typology.type: The words carved for ever, 19:23 to 24
typology.fulfillment: Job wishes his testimony to be inscribed in a book and cut in stone. The wish was granted in a way he could not have foreseen: his words are in Scripture, read by countless generations, and cited by the apostles, as in 1 Corinthians 3:19 and James 5:11. The pattern is of a private cry becoming a public witness. The escalation is that the Word Himself became flesh, John 1:14, and His words are living, John 6:63. The type is limited in that Job's book is a record of suffering, while Christ's is a record that gives life.

study.christ:
Job's confession leads to Christ first by the office he names. The go'el was the family member who paid what the helpless could not. Job, cut off from every relative, looks for one who will stand with him, and says that this one lives. The New Testament declares who that is. Christ took on the family likeness, 'since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity', Hebrews 2:14, and was 'born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law', Galatians 4:4 to 5. Peter says we were redeemed 'with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot', 1 Peter 1:19, and Paul that He 'gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness', Titus 2:14. What Job could name only as a role is now a name.

It leads to Christ in the word 'lives'. Job does not say his Redeemer lived, or once acted. He says lives. The living God, whose life Job swears by in 27:2, is not a memory. In the gospel this is embodied: 'I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever! And I hold the keys of Death and of Hades', Revelation 1:18. The one who rose is the Redeemer who lives.

It leads to Christ by the promise of the body. Job holds that he will see God in his own flesh, and Jesus rose in flesh that could be touched, Luke 24:39. Paul argues that this is not merely a hope for one man: 'Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep', 1 Corinthians 15:20. The harvest that Job expects follows the firstfruits that Christ is. The Redeemer's standing upon the dust is echoed in the empty tomb.

It leads to Christ in the estrangement that Job feels and Christ bears. Psalm 69:8 speaks of being a stranger to one's brothers, and it is applied to Christ, since His own brothers did not believe in Him, John 7:5, and His disciples fled, Mark 14:50. The Redeemer is one who knows the isolation of Job from inside. And the promise of seeing God 'and not as a stranger' becomes the promise that believers, once far off, are brought near, Ephesians 2:13.

The care needed is that Job's own knowledge was partial. He stands in the dark with a light he cannot fully explain, and it would be wrong to make him a New Testament preacher. What we can say is that the Spirit who inspired the book gave words that fit the gospel more closely than the speaker could have known, and that the New Testament fulfils them.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is at once the cause of Job's grief and the object of his hope, and the chapter does not blur the two. Job says that God has wronged him and drawn a net around him, has blocked his way, stripped his crown and uprooted his hope, and counts him as an enemy. Then in the same speech he says his Redeemer lives. The Bible allows a believer to hold both, and it does not call either a lie. It is the raw form of what later Scripture calls faith.

The chapter shows God as one who is alive and who acts. In Job's confession the key word is that the Redeemer lives. In a book where the friends have offered a system of consequences, Job clings to a person. The God he hopes in is not a principle of justice but a living one who will rise, stand, and be seen.

It also shows a God who is faithful to the weak. The go'el is the one who does not leave the helpless to their own resources. When God is called Redeemer in Isaiah 41:14 and 54:5, it is this loyalty to a people with no strength of their own that is meant. Job, without knowing how, is leaning on that character.

There is a truth about God's justice as well. The chapter closes with the warning that there is a judgment, verse 29. The same God who will redeem the sufferer will hold accusers to account, and Job 42:7 confirms this, as God speaks in anger against the three friends. His care for the wronged and his severity toward the false comforter are two sides of the same holiness.

And there is a truth about God's nearness. Job hopes to see Him 'not as a stranger'. The God of Scripture is not remote, and the whole story bends toward the day when His people see His face, Revelation 22:4.

For worship, the passage teaches that the deepest praise can be sung from the ash heap. It teaches the language of trust that survives contradiction: I know that my Redeemer lives. And it invites us to hold to that confession when we cannot explain God's hand, and to say with Job that we will see Him for ourselves.

crossReferences.note: The earlier wish for a mediator who could lay his hand on both. Chapter 19 is the point where that longing becomes a confident statement that a Redeemer lives, and it shows how patiently the book raises the question before it lets Job say his answer.

Job pictures being hidden in Sheol until God remembers him, and asks if a man who dies will live again, then waits for his renewal. Chapter 19 is the fuller reply to that earlier question, moving from an unanswered 'if' to a settled 'I know'.

The witness in heaven and the plea that a man might argue with God as with a neighbour. Chapter 19 sharpens these into the person of the Redeemer, and reading the two passages together shows a single hope being drawn out step by step.

If a person sells himself into slavery, a relative may redeem him. This law gives the go'el his job: to rescue a relative from bondage. It shows why Job's word carries such weight for a man who has lost everything, including his standing in his household.

Boaz publicly takes on the duty of the kinsman-redeemer, buying the land and taking Ruth, so that the dead man's name will not be cut off. The story shows the goodness of the office and the cost borne by the redeemer, and it gives Job's word a face.

The LORD says to Jacob, 'Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel.' Here the title is given to God Himself, which is why many read Job's Redeemer as God. It also shows the go'el role stretched to cover a whole people's helplessness.

The psalmist is held by God's right hand, guided by His counsel, and later received in glory. Like Job, he holds to God when circumstances contradict him, and he looks beyond death. The two passages mark the same road out of despair.

Christ has been raised as the firstfruits, and those who belong to Him will follow. This turns Job's personal hope of bodily vindication into a promise for all believers, grounded in an event that has already happened.
'We will see Him as He is.' John's language matches Job's hope of seeing God with his own eyes, and it gives the ground: we are already God's children, and we shall be like Him when He appears.

The risen Christ is the Living One, holding the keys of Death and Hades. The Redeemer who lives in Job's confession has a name and a nail-marked hand here. It is the answer to the fear of death which Job's whole speech was pressing against.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with a world where God and humanity meet face to face, and the fall in Genesis 3 puts a barrier between them. From then on the story is a search for a way back: a promise of a seed, a covenant, a sacrificial system, a priesthood, and a longing that the people of God repeat in one form after another. Job 19 is one of the clearest pictures of that longing, and it comes from someone outside Israel's covenant history, which shows how deep the need runs.

What the chapter answers from before is the question of what happens to a righteous person who dies. Genesis had said that to dust we return, and Job 14 had wondered whether a man who dies can live again. The friends have no answer. Job's answer is not a theory but a person: my Redeemer lives.

What the chapter sets up is the entire biblical hope of resurrection and of seeing God. The Psalms voice it, Psalm 16:10, 49:15, 73:24, and the prophets state it plainly, Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2. Then it is embodied. The God who took flesh, John 1:14, died as the go'el of a family that could not pay, and was raised as the firstfruits, 1 Corinthians 15:20. The Redeemer stood on the dust in Bethlehem and on Golgotha, and stood again out of the tomb.

The chapter also warns about how the story is carried. Job's friends are religious men who protect a system and lose the person in front of them. The go'el is the one who does not. The people of God are meant to be a family in which no one is left to the mercy of the world, and where a widow or a sufferer finds someone who steps in.

The story ends where Job's hope was aimed. Paul says that this mortal body will be clothed with immortality, 1 Corinthians 15:53, and John sees God's people with His face before them, Revelation 22:4. The isolation of Job 19 is reversed: the estranged are welcomed, and the accusers of the brothers are thrown down, Revelation 12:10. The one who lives stands on a renewed earth, and His people see Him for themselves, and not as strangers.

sermon.title: Holding on to Your Faith in the Midst of Suffering: Job, Part 2
sermon.why: Piper devotes an extended section of this message to Job 19:25-27, tracing Job's progress of faith from despair over death in chapter 7 to this climactic confession, showing that Job's Redeemer is God Himself and, from the New Testament's vantage point, ultimately Christ who redeemed him.

quiz.q: How complete is Job's isolation described in 19:13-19?

options.text: Total: his brothers, acquaintances, kinsmen, servants, wife, and even children now treat him as a stranger or mock him.
options.note: This catalog of abandonment, verses 13-19, is one of the most comprehensive pictures of isolation in the Bible.

options.text: Nearly complete, extending even to his own household and closest family, though the text does not mention every relationship.
options.note: Close to the chapter's actual scope, though less complete than its explicit naming of brothers, wife, servants, and children alike.

options.text: Job exaggerates for rhetorical effect but is not truly isolated.
options.note: The text presents this catalog as Job's genuine experience within the narrative, not merely rhetorical exaggeration.

options.text: Only his servants have abandoned him.
options.note: The passage names brothers, acquaintances, kinsmen, his wife, and even children, far broader than servants alone.

quiz.q: What does Job declare in his climactic statement in 19:25?

options.text: That he knows his Redeemer lives and will, in the end, stand upon the earth.
options.note: This is the chapter's central and most quoted declaration of hope.

options.text: That someone living will one day rise to vindicate him, even though he cannot yet see how.
options.note: A true summary of Job's hope, though less precise than his exact confession that his Redeemer lives and will stand upon the earth.

options.text: That his friends will finally repent of their accusations.
options.note: Job's declaration in verse 25 concerns his Redeemer, not a prediction about his friends' future repentance, though he does warn them of coming judgment in verses 28-29.

options.text: That he no longer believes in any form of justice.
options.note: This is the opposite of Job's actual declaration, which is a bold statement of hope and trust.

quiz.q: What does Job hope for regarding his own body in 19:26?

options.text: That even after his skin is destroyed, he will see God in his own flesh.
options.note: This hope reaches toward bodily vindication, not merely a disembodied spiritual comfort.

options.text: That his own eyes will behold God, not as a stranger, after his present body is gone.
options.note: A true part of Job's hope in verse 27, though less exact than his direct claim in verse 26 of seeing God in his flesh.

options.text: That his body will be preserved exactly as it currently is, covered in boils.
options.note: Job's hope is for vindication and seeing God after his body's destruction, not for preservation of his current diseased state.

options.text: That only his soul, not his body, will survive.
options.note: Job specifically hopes to see God in his flesh, indicating a bodily rather than purely disembodied hope.

quiz.q: What is the meaning and background of the term 'Redeemer' (go'el) in 19:25?

options.text: It refers to a kinsman-redeemer, a family member with the legal right and duty to rescue or avenge a relative in distress, a role Job applies here directly to God.
options.note: This legal and family category, seen clearly in the book of Ruth, is the background for Job's bold application of the term to God Himself.

options.text: It refers to someone with a recognized right to rescue and vindicate another, most fully seen in the book of Ruth.
options.note: Correct as far as it goes, though less specific than naming the exact family and legal obligation Job draws on when applying this title to God.

options.text: It refers to a hired legal advocate with no family connection.
options.note: The go'el specifically carries family or kinship obligation, distinct from a hired, unrelated legal advocate.

options.text: It is a term exclusively used for financial transactions with no personal rescue implied.
options.note: While the go'el could redeem property, the term also carries the sense of personal rescue and vindication, which is Job's primary use here.

quiz.q: How does this chapter's hope connect to the New Testament's teaching about Christ?

options.text: It anticipates Christ as the living Redeemer, both kinsman through His incarnation and Redeemer through His death and resurrection, who guarantees bodily resurrection for believers.
options.note: This connection, drawn out in passages like 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 and Revelation 1:17-18, is one of the clearest typological threads in the book of Job.

options.text: It points forward to a risen, living figure who will one day stand visibly among His people, an image later fulfilled and clarified in Christ.
options.note: Correct in its general direction, though less precise than naming the specific New Testament passages and doctrine of bodily resurrection this hope anticipates.

options.text: It is fulfilled completely by Job's earthly restoration in chapter 42.
options.note: While Job is restored in this life by chapter 42, his hope here reaches toward something beyond mere earthly restoration, toward seeing God Himself in resurrected flesh.

options.text: It has no connection to the New Testament's teaching on Christ.
options.note: This passage is widely recognized as one of the Old Testament's clearest anticipations of the hope fulfilled in Christ.

questions: Job's hope in a living Redeemer breaks out suddenly, in the middle of total isolation, not after his circumstances improved. Where might you need to voice hope in Christ even while your own circumstances remain unresolved?
Job's own family and closest friends turned against him in his suffering. Have you ever experienced isolation from people you expected to stand by you, and how did you keep trusting God through it?

Job hopes not just for spiritual comfort but to see God in his own flesh, a bodily hope. How does the promise of bodily resurrection, not just 'going to heaven,' shape the way you think about your own future or grieve the loss of others?

Job wished his words could be inscribed in stone forever, and in a sense they have been, preserved in Scripture for thousands of years. What words or convictions do you hold now that you hope will outlast your present circumstances?

Job calls God both his adversary, who has wronged him, and his Redeemer, who lives. How do you hold together your honest complaints to God with your deepest trust in Him, without needing to resolve the tension first?

translationNotes.note: Job's wish that his words be inscribed with an iron stylus on lead, or chiseled in stone, describes ancient methods of creating a permanent, indestructible record, a wish remarkably fulfilled by this speech's permanent place in Scripture.

Redeemer renders go'el, the kinsman-redeemer of Israelite family law, most vividly illustrated in the book of Ruth; Job's application of this family category to God is a bold theological move reaching beyond any human redeemer available to him.

This verse is one of the most textually and grammatically debated in the Old Testament; the BSB's rendering, in my flesh I will see God, reflects the reading that affirms Job's hope of bodily vindication, the interpretation followed by most historic Christian commentary.
